classification_reason: A common, productive verb for holding tightly and continuing to hold a belief, hope, or habit.

senses.definition: To hold tightly to someone or something.
senses.example: The wet fabric clung to her skin.
senses.usage_note: Common pattern: cling to someone or something. The past tense and past participle are clung.

synonyms.note: usually takes a direct object, while cling is normally followed by to

senses.definition: To continue believing in or depending on something, especially when it is no longer helpful or likely.
senses.example: Some managers still cling to outdated working practices.
senses.usage_note: Common combinations include cling to hope, cling to power, and cling to the past.

synonyms.note: more conversational and often less negative

antonyms.note: means to stop holding, depending on, or emotionally retaining something

classification_reason: A vivid motion verb commonly understood in stories and descriptions, especially for children and small animals, but less important for general production.

senses.definition: To run quickly with small, light steps, especially like a child or small animal.
senses.example: A squirrel scampered across the roof and disappeared into a tree.

synonyms.note: often suggests hurried or nervous movement

classification_reason: A useful concrete noun in descriptions of forests, beds, vehicles, and outdoor structures, but mainly needed for recognition.

senses.definition: A covering fixed above a bed, seat, entrance, or outdoor area.
senses.example: A canvas canopy protected the diners from the afternoon sun.

senses.definition: The upper layer of branches and leaves formed by trees in a forest.
senses.example: Very little sunlight reaches the ground beneath the rainforest canopy.

classification_reason: A practical word for materials that bond surfaces, useful in everyday instructions and technical discussions.

senses.definition: A substance used to make surfaces stick together.
senses.example: The technician used a heat-resistant adhesive to attach the sensor.

synonyms.note: an everyday word for many, but not all, types of adhesive

senses.definition: Able or intended to stick firmly to a surface.
senses.example: Remove the protective film before applying the adhesive strip.

synonyms.note: broader and more informal; it may describe an unwanted texture

classification_reason: A broadly useful scientific and figurative adjective for things that are extremely small.

senses.definition: So small that it can be seen only with a microscope.
senses.example: Researchers found microscopic fibers in the water sample.

senses.definition: Extremely small in amount, size, or importance.
senses.example: The software update produced only a microscopic improvement in performance.

synonyms.note: much broader and less emphatic

classification_reason: A useful everyday noun for the bottom of a foot or shoe and a productive adjective meaning only.

senses.definition: The bottom surface of a foot or shoe.
senses.example: The soles of the boots provide a firm grip on wet rocks.

senses.definition: Being the only one or the only thing of a particular kind.
senses.example: Cost was not the sole reason for delaying the project.

synonyms.note: more common and has a wider range of grammatical uses

classification_reason: A highly productive verb for drawing people, attention, investment, and physical objects toward something.

senses.definition: To cause someone to become interested in, visit, or choose something.
senses.example: The flexible schedule helped the company attract experienced engineers.
senses.usage_note: Common combinations include attract attention, attract customers, and be attracted to someone or something.

synonyms.note: often used with attention, interest, crowds, and criticism

senses.definition: To pull an object toward another object through a physical force.
senses.example: Oppositely charged particles attract each other.
senses.usage_note: The passive pattern be attracted to describes the direction of the force.

synonyms.note: broader and does not necessarily describe attraction between objects

antonyms.note: means to push an object away through a physical force

classification_reason: A very common time noun with a distinct adjective pronunciation and meaning, plus an important professional plural sense in meeting minutes.

senses.definition: A unit of time equal to 60 seconds, or a short period of time.
senses.example: Could we discuss the deployment plan for a minute?

senses.definition: An official written record of what was discussed or decided at a meeting, normally used in the plural.
senses.example: I reviewed the meeting minutes before assigning the action items.
senses.usage_note: This sense is normally plural: the minutes of a meeting or meeting minutes.

senses.definition: Extremely small.
senses.example: The sensor can detect minute changes in air pressure.
senses.usage_note: This adjective is pronounced /maɪˈnut/, unlike the time noun /ˈmɪnət/.

synonyms.note: more common and less formal

classification_reason: A common biological category worth recognizing in reading and general conversation, but with limited productive value for the learner's main goals.

senses.definition: A cold-blooded vertebrate with scales, such as a snake, lizard, turtle, or crocodile.
senses.example: Unlike most reptiles, some species of gecko are active during the day.

classification_reason: A standard anatomical noun useful for understanding health, biology, and movement descriptions, but mainly needed receptively.

senses.definition: The bony structure at the base of the spine that connects the upper body to the legs.
senses.example: The physical therapist showed her how to keep her pelvis level while walking.

classification_reason: A very common everyday noun with broadly useful structural, scientific, and geological senses.

senses.definition: A flat, usually round dish used for serving or eating food.
senses.example: She filled her plate with vegetables and grilled chicken.

senses.definition: A thin, flat piece or layer of a hard material such as metal, glass, or bone.
senses.example: A steel plate reinforced the damaged section of the bridge.

senses.definition: One of the large moving sections of Earth's outer layer.
senses.example: Earthquakes frequently occur near the boundaries of tectonic plates.

classification_reason: A useful descriptive adverb for firm physical attachment or persistent effort, but less common than the adjective tenacious.

senses.definition: With a very firm grip or attachment.
senses.example: The gecko clung tenaciously to the smooth glass.

synonyms.note: more common and less emphatic

senses.definition: With persistent determination; without giving up easily.
senses.example: The research team pursued the problem tenaciously for several years.

synonyms.note: emphasizes continuing an effort rather than refusing to let go

classification_reason: A recognizable noun for groups of three, common in journalism, music, and descriptive writing but not essential for active production.

senses.definition: A group of three people or things, especially three musicians who perform together.
senses.example: A trio of engineers presented the prototype to the client.
senses.usage_note: Common pattern: a trio of people or things.

classification_reason: A useful everyday weather and spray noun with a practical verb sense.

senses.definition: A cloud of extremely small drops of water in the air, usually less dense than fog.
senses.example: A light mist covered the harbor early in the morning.

synonyms.note: usually denser and more likely to reduce visibility

senses.definition: A mass of very small drops of a liquid produced by a spray.
senses.example: A fine mist of disinfectant settled over the surface.

synonyms.note: broader and can contain larger drops

senses.definition: To cover something with very small drops of liquid.
senses.example: Mist the leaves lightly when the soil begins to dry out.

synonyms.note: broader and does not necessarily imply very fine drops

classification_reason: A specialized but recognizable scientific adjective useful in materials, chemistry, and biological descriptions.

senses.definition: Tending to repel water or not mix with water.
senses.example: The hydrophobic coating causes water to form droplets on the glass.

synonyms.note: a more practical description, while hydrophobic is the technical term for the material property

classification_reason: A useful word for materials that resist substances, products that keep pests away, and things that cause strong disgust.

senses.definition: Able to prevent a substance, insect, or other thing from approaching or being absorbed.
senses.example: The jacket is made from a water-repellent fabric.
senses.usage_note: Often used after a noun in compounds such as water-repellent and insect-repellent.

synonyms.note: usually combines with a noun using resistant to, as in resistant to water

senses.definition: Causing strong dislike or disgust.
senses.example: The committee described the discriminatory policy as morally repellent.

synonyms.note: more common and less formal

senses.definition: A substance used to keep insects, animals, or water away.
senses.example: We applied insect repellent before entering the forest.
senses.usage_note: Common combinations include insect repellent and water repellent.

classification_reason: A recognizable descriptive adjective for a silver-like color or shine, useful mainly in reading and visual description.

senses.definition: Similar to silver in color or shine.
senses.example: A silvery bubble formed around the insect's body underwater.

synonyms.note: more literal and less descriptive

classification_reason: A productive academic and professional verb for forced relocation, replacement, and the physical movement of matter.

senses.definition: To force people to leave their homes or usual location.
senses.example: The flooding displaced thousands of residents from coastal communities.

synonyms.note: more direct and less formal

senses.definition: To take the position, role, or function previously held by someone or something else.
senses.example: Automation may displace some routine administrative jobs.

synonyms.note: focuses on what takes the old thing's place, while displace focuses on what is removed

senses.definition: To move something from its normal position or cause a substance to occupy a different space.
senses.example: The object displaced an equal volume of water when it was submerged.

synonyms.note: much broader and does not imply removal from an existing position

classification_reason: A common adjective for describing something that is slightly wet, useful in everyday conversation and descriptions.

senses.definition: Slightly wet; not completely wet.
senses.example: The morning mist left my jacket damp.

synonyms.note: often more neutral or positive, especially for food, skin, and soil
broader and usually indicates more water

classification_reason: A productive expression for something that is very close to happening, useful in conversation, IELTS, and professional discussion.

senses.definition: Very close to experiencing a state or having something happen.
senses.example: The startup was on the verge of shutting down when it secured new funding.
senses.usage_note: Use on the verge of plus a noun or an -ing form, not an infinitive.

synonyms.note: often used for serious, dangerous, or dramatic situations
followed by a base verb rather than of plus a noun or -ing form

classification_reason: A vivid and useful verb for making someone or something completely wet.

senses.definition: To make someone or something completely wet, usually with a large amount of liquid.
senses.example: The sudden downpour drenched everyone waiting for the bus.

synonyms.note: can also mean to leave something in liquid for a period of time

classification_reason: A useful verb for dishonest manipulation and equipment setup, with common technical noun senses; the submitted form was normalized from rigged to rig.

senses.definition: To control or arrange a result dishonestly so that someone gains an unfair advantage.
senses.example: Several contractors were accused of rigging the bidding process.

synonyms.note: has this meaning in combinations such as fix a match or election
broader and not always dishonest

senses.definition: To equip or arrange something for a particular purpose.
senses.example: The crew rigged the camera with a safety cable before filming.

synonyms.note: more neutral and does not suggest a custom arrangement
broader and often used for complete systems

senses.definition: Equipment or a structure assembled for a particular purpose.
senses.example: The camera operator carried a lightweight shoulder rig.

synonyms.note: broader and less focused on physical equipment

senses.definition: A large truck, especially a tractor-trailer.
senses.example: A big rig pulled into the highway rest area.
senses.usage_note: American English; especially common in the expression big rig.

synonyms.note: more precise and neutral
